article_title: How to Spot a Refurbished Phone Listed as New
claim: Checking the IMEI against India's Central Equipment Identity Register (CEIR) tells you whether a device has ever been reported lost, stolen, or blacklisted.
source: CEIR / Sanchar Saathi (Department of Telecommunications, Government of India)
required_correction: None — CEIR (now integrated into the Sanchar Saathi portal, ceir.sancharsaathi.gov.in) lets citizens verify IMEI status (valid/blacklisted/duplicate) and also lets owners block/report lost or stolen phones. Article could add the exact portal name (Sanchar Saathi) since 'ceir.gov.in' redirects there and the branding has changed.

article_title: How to Spot a Refurbished Phone Listed as New
claim: iPhones show battery health, including cycle count, directly under Settings > Battery > Battery Health.
source: Apple Support
required_correction: None for older/current iPhones broadly — accurate. Minor nuance: on iPhone 15 and later running iOS 17.4+, cycle count is shown directly in Settings > Battery > Battery Health; on iPhone 14 and earlier, or older iOS versions, cycle count requires the Settings > Privacy & Security > Analytics Data workaround since it isn't shown on-screen by default. Article should note this model/iOS-version caveat rather than implying it's uniformly on-screen for all iPhones.

article_title: How to Spot a Refurbished Phone Listed as New
claim: A brand-new phone's battery should show at or very close to 100 percent health with zero, one, or two charge cycles.
source: Apple Support (battery and performance documentation)
required_correction: Directionally correct and consistent with how battery health/cycle count is defined, but no manufacturer publishes an official 'must be 100% with 0-2 cycles to count as new' threshold — a phone that sat in a warehouse or was demoed briefly can legitimately show a handful of cycles and slightly under 100% without being refurbished. Soften to 'should be very close to' rather than implying an exact pass/fail number.

article_title: How to Spot a Refurbished Phone Listed as New
claim: Flipkart and Amazon India both specify a return or replacement window per listing, and it is frequently shorter for phones, sometimes as little as seven days.
source: Flipkart Return Policy page; reporting on Amazon India's smartphone return policy change
required_correction: Flipkart's own policy confirms a 7-day replacement window for mobile phones (15-day return for select premium phones, excluding iPhone/Google Pixel from returns). Amazon India has moved further than the article implies: for most mobile phones Amazon now offers replacement-only (no refund-return) for confirmed manufacturing defects, not a simple 'return window' — the article should clarify replacement vs. return distinction rather than treating both platforms as offering the same kind of window.

article_title: How to Spot a Refurbished Phone Listed as New
claim: Imported/international-variant refurbished units sold as domestic stock can lack official Indian warranty support entirely and can differ in supported network bands.
source: General consensus across manufacturer warranty terms (e.g., Apple, Samsung region-locked warranty policies) — no single authoritative Indian government source found
required_correction: The underlying mechanism (region-locked warranty, band variance) is well established industry practice, but no single official regulator source lists which specific bands or warranty exclusions apply across brands, so this should be treated as generally accurate but not centrally documented — attribute to 'varies by brand and model' rather than a blanket rule.

article_title: How to Spot a Refurbished Phone Listed as New
claim: A price below the standard street price for that exact model, outside a known sale event, is the single strongest signal something is off.
required_correction: Editorial judgment/heuristic, not an independently checkable fact. Reasonable advice but presented with more certainty ('the single strongest signal') than can be substantiated.

article_title: How to Spot a Refurbished Phone Listed as New
claim: Check the factory screen protector for bubbling, the back glass under angled light for micro-scratches, and the charging port for dust or wear as physical tells of prior use.
required_correction: Practical, plausible advice but subjective/anecdotal rather than a verifiable standard — no authoritative source defines these as reliable refurbishment indicators, and the article itself concedes they're 'not conclusive alone.'

article_title: How to Spot a Refurbished Phone Listed as New
claim: Genuine new phones ship with a specific, documented set of accessories for that exact model and region, and a missing cable or generic charger is a sign of swapped packaging.
required_correction: Generally sound consumer advice but not an independently checkable statistic — box contents vary by region/regulatory changes (e.g., many brands no longer ship chargers at all in some markets), so the claim should note that 'no charger in box' is now often normal, not automatically a red flag.

article_title: How Much RAM You Actually Need in a Laptop in 2026
claim: Electron-based apps (Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Notion) can individually use several hundred megabytes to over a gigabyte of memory just sitting open in the background.
source: Multiple independent reporting/benchmarks (Hacker News discussion threads, technical write-ups on Electron memory usage) — no single vendor publishes official idle-RAM figures
required_correction: None on the range itself — widely and consistently reported that Slack/Discord/Teams commonly sit at 400MB-2GB+ after some use, consistent with the article's 'several hundred MB to over a gigabyte' framing. Note this is an industry-observation claim, not something with one authoritative source, since Electron/vendors don't publish official memory-use specs.

article_title: How Much RAM You Actually Need in a Laptop in 2026
claim: Every open browser tab runs largely as its own process with its own memory allocation, and extensions add further overhead.
source: Google Chrome multi-process architecture documentation
required_correction: None — Chromium's (and by extension Chrome/Edge/Brave) documented multi-process architecture assigns separate renderer processes per tab/site-instance by default, which is the technical basis for the claim. Firefox uses a similar but more limited multi-process model, so 'largely as its own process' is accurate as a generalization across major browsers.

article_title: How Much RAM You Actually Need in a Laptop in 2026
claim: Windows Task Manager's Memory tab and macOS Activity Monitor both show real-time usage broken down by app and process, sortable by memory.
source: Microsoft Support (Task Manager) and Apple Support (Activity Monitor)
required_correction: None — both are documented, built-in system utilities and both support sorting the process list by memory usage.

article_title: How Much RAM You Actually Need in a Laptop in 2026
claim: When physical RAM fills up, the OS uses disk space as swap/virtual memory, which is dramatically slower than real RAM even on a fast SSD.
source: Established computer architecture principle (documented across OS vendor and hardware technical documentation)
required_correction: None — this is a well-established, non-controversial computing fact: even the fastest consumer NVMe SSDs are orders of magnitude slower than RAM in latency, so swap usage causes noticeable slowdown. No single citable URL needed as this is foundational computer science, not a disputed or vendor-specific claim.

article_title: How Much RAM You Actually Need in a Laptop in 2026
claim: A large share of modern thin-and-light laptops solder RAM directly to the motherboard, meaning there is no upgrade path after purchase.
source: General industry knowledge (widely reported across laptop teardown/reviews, e.g., ultrabooks and MacBooks since 2020 using soldered LPDDR RAM) — no single regulator or vendor index tracks 'share' of models
required_correction: Directionally accurate — soldered RAM is now standard on most premium/thin-and-light lines (MacBooks, XPS, many ultraportables), but 'a large share' is an estimate with no precise industry-wide statistic behind it, and many budget/business laptops (ThinkPad, some HP/Dell lines) still ship with SO-DIMM slots. Soften the claim to avoid implying a specific measured proportion.

article_title: How Much RAM You Actually Need in a Laptop in 2026
claim: 8GB is workable for basic browsing/office work but tight for multitasking; 16GB is the comfortable baseline for most users in 2026; 32GB is needed for local AI inference, video editing, VMs/Docker, or heavy multitasking.
required_correction: This is an editorial recommendation/buying-guide judgment, not an independently checkable fact — reasonable given the Electron/browser memory data above, but presented as a settled tier system when actual comfortable RAM varies significantly by specific workload and OS.

article_title: How Much RAM You Actually Need in a Laptop in 2026
claim: Modern versions of Windows, macOS, and ChromeOS all run more background services, indexing, sync processes, and security features than their equivalents did five years ago.
required_correction: Plausible general trend but no measured, citable comparison (e.g., idle RAM footprint of Windows 10 vs. Windows 11, or macOS versions five years apart) was found to substantiate this as stated. Should be softened to an editorial observation rather than presented as an established fact.

article_title: Smartwatch Buying Guide: Which Features Are Worth Paying Extra For
claim: A watch with its own built-in GPS chip can track an outdoor run or ride accurately without the phone nearby; a watch without one relies on the phone's GPS over Bluetooth.
source: General smartwatch/wearable GPS architecture, consistent across major vendor documentation (Garmin, Apple, Samsung)
required_correction: None — this is standard, well-documented smartwatch design: 'connected GPS' watches use the paired phone's GPS radio while 'built-in GPS' watches have their own chip and antenna. Consistently described this way across vendor spec sheets.

article_title: Smartwatch Buying Guide: Which Features Are Worth Paying Extra For
claim: SpO2 and ECG sensors on consumer smartwatches are useful for spotting trends but aren't certified medical diagnostic devices and shouldn't be treated as one.
source: Apple (Blood Oxygen app disclaimer) and Samsung (Galaxy Watch health disclaimers)
required_correction: Accurate for SpO2 (Apple explicitly states Blood Oxygen readings are 'not intended for medical use' and are wellness-only). ECG is a partial exception: Apple Watch's ECG app IS FDA-cleared (De Novo classification) specifically for detecting atrial fibrillation and is a legitimate over-the-counter medical feature for that one purpose — but it explicitly cannot detect heart attacks and isn't a general diagnostic tool. Article should distinguish that ECG has narrow FDA clearance for AFib detection, while SpO2 generally does not have equivalent medical clearance.

article_title: Smartwatch Buying Guide: Which Features Are Worth Paying Extra For
claim: An IP68 rating covers dust and splash resistance but isn't built for swimming; a 5ATM rating is tested for sustained water pressure at depth and is what's needed for swimming.
source: ISO 22810:2010 (water-resistant watches standard); Samsung Global Newsroom
required_correction: None on the core distinction — IP68 is an ingress-protection (dust/static submersion) test under IEC 60529, while 5ATM/ISO 22810 includes condensation, temperature, and static overpressure testing more relevant to swimming. Worth adding the nuance that even 5ATM is a static-pressure test and doesn't fully account for dynamic forces like diving entry or strong swimming strokes, so brands still often advise against high-impact water sports even at 5ATM.

article_title: Smartwatch Buying Guide: Which Features Are Worth Paying Extra For
claim: A cellular smartwatch requires a real cost premium and often an added monthly charge from the carrier.
source: Airtel eSIM for smartwatches page
required_correction: Partially misleading as a blanket statement for India: while cellular watches generally cost more upfront (accurate), the 'added monthly charge' isn't universal — Airtel, for example, offers smartwatch eSIM service free with certain existing postpaid plans (My Plan/Infinity), not as a guaranteed extra monthly fee. Article should note it depends on the carrier and existing plan rather than presenting an added monthly charge as a given.

article_title: Smartwatch Buying Guide: Which Features Are Worth Paying Extra For
claim: Simpler fitness-band style wearables commonly run five to seven days on a charge; full-featured smartwatches with always-on AMOLED, GPS, and constant health tracking often need charging every one to two days.
required_correction: Directionally reasonable as a generalization but stated as a firm fact with no cited source or specific models — real battery life varies enormously by brand and specific model (some full-featured AMOLED smartwatches, e.g. Amazfit/Garmin lines, claim 5+ days; some basic bands last 2 weeks+). Should be attributed as a rough rule of thumb, or replaced with named model examples and their official specs.

article_title: Smartwatch Buying Guide: Which Features Are Worth Paying Extra For
claim: A physical rotating bezel or crown makes the watch usable with wet or gloved hands and during workouts when touchscreen accuracy drops.
required_correction: Reasonable usability judgment but subjective, not independently checkable against a source.

article_title: Smartwatch Buying Guide: Which Features Are Worth Paying Extra For
claim: Some smartwatches use a proprietary band attachment that locks buyers into buying replacement bands only from that brand, often at a premium.
required_correction: Broadly true as a category statement (e.g., Apple Watch's proprietary band system vs. standard lug-width watches) but framed generally without naming which brands/models, making it more of an editorial generalization than a specific verifiable claim.

article_title: How to Check a Product's Real Reviews Instead of Fake Ones
claim: Paid reviewers now routinely buy the product for real, post the review, and get refunded separately outside the platform, earning the verified purchase badge without it costing them anything.
source: Amazon's own reporting on fake-review-broker lawsuits; The Hustle investigative report
required_correction: None — Amazon's own legal actions describe exactly this pattern (buy, post 5-star review, receive refund/payment via PayPal or gift card outside Amazon, sometimes with a commission), and Amazon has sued multiple review-broker networks (Lotstrade, ReviewerAgency, AppSally, Rebatest) organizing hundreds of thousands of participants in this scheme.

article_title: How to Check a Product's Real Reviews Instead of Fake Ones
claim: A verified purchase badge still filters out a meaningful share of reviews from people who never bought the product at all.
source: Amazon Verified Purchase badge policy (community guidelines)
required_correction: None — Amazon's Verified Purchase badge is only applied when the reviewer purchased the item at a reasonably close-to-retail price through Amazon, which does mechanically exclude reviews from accounts that never purchased through the platform, even though it doesn't stop the buy-then-refund workaround described in the prior claim.

article_title: How to Check a Product's Real Reviews Instead of Fake Ones
claim: Reviews in the three-star range tend to be the most detailed and balanced, written by people with specific, mixed feedback rather than a blanket reaction.
required_correction: Presented as a general rule but it's a heuristic/opinion about review psychology, not an independently checkable statistic — no cited study on review-detail-by-star-rating was found to back this as a firm pattern.

article_title: How to Check a Product's Real Reviews Instead of Fake Ones
claim: A sudden cluster of five-star reviews posted within a few days of each other, especially soon after a listing goes live, is a common pattern for a coordinated review campaign.
required_correction: Plausible and consistent with how Amazon itself describes detecting review manipulation (pattern/timing analysis), but no specific authoritative source was found confirming 'a few days' as a defined threshold — Amazon's own detection systems use proprietary signals not publicly documented in that level of detail. Present as a reasonable heuristic, not a confirmed detection rule.

article_title: How to Check a Product's Real Reviews Instead of Fake Ones
claim: A product sitting at 4.3 stars across ten thousand reviews has statistically absorbed far more genuine buyer experience than one at a suspiciously perfect 4.9 across only two hundred.
required_correction: A statistical intuition presented as guidance, not a checkable fact — the specific numbers (4.3/10,000 vs 4.9/200) are illustrative examples, not a cited statistic.

article_title: How to Check a Product's Real Reviews Instead of Fake Ones
claim: A reverse image search on the main product photo occasionally reveals the same generic product sold under several different brand names at different price points.
required_correction: Reads as a plausible, widely-known technique (rebranded/whitelabel products on Indian marketplaces are a documented phenomenon) but is presented generically without a specific example or source, giving it a generic/unverified feel rather than a demonstrated case.

article_title: How to Check a Product's Real Reviews Instead of Fake Ones
claim: A new listing that accumulates hundreds of reviews within its first week, before the product has plausibly been used long enough for genuine feedback to form, is a strong sign of purchased or incentivized reviews.
required_correction: Reasonable heuristic consistent with how review manipulation is generally described, but no specific, cited threshold or study defines 'hundreds within a week' as a formal red flag — treat as editorial judgment rather than an established detection rule.

article_title: How to Tell If Your Internet Plan Is Actually Giving You the Speed You Pay For
claim: Testing over Wi-Fi introduces its own bottlenecks; connecting a laptop directly to the router via Ethernet and testing gives a more accurate read of what the ISP is actually delivering.
source: Ookla Speedtest guidance / methodology reporting
required_correction: None — wired testing to eliminate Wi-Fi interference and device-chip limitations is standard, widely recommended methodology consistent with Ookla's own guidance.

article_title: How to Tell If Your Internet Plan Is Actually Giving You the Speed You Pay For
claim: Speed test sites connect to a nearby server, and results can vary depending on which server you land on and how busy it is, so it's worth running the test on at least two different services.
source: Ookla Speedtest server-selection methodology
required_correction: None — Ookla's own documentation confirms tests connect to one of many thousands of partner servers and that server choice and load affect results, which is the basis for recommending cross-checking with more than one tool/server.

article_title: How to Tell If Your Internet Plan Is Actually Giving You the Speed You Pay For
claim: ISPs sell bandwidth based on a contention ratio; the advertised speed is a maximum, not a guaranteed constant, shared to some degree with other users on the same local infrastructure.
source: TRAI (Telecom Regulatory Authority of India) broadband policy framework
required_correction: None — contention/oversubscription is standard, disclosed industry practice, and ISP-advertised speeds in India (and globally) are consistently framed as 'up to' maximums rather than guaranteed constants, consistent with TRAI's own broadband guidance framework.

article_title: How to Tell If Your Internet Plan Is Actually Giving You the Speed You Pay For
claim: Some broadband plans throttle speed after a certain monthly data threshold is crossed under a Fair Usage Policy.
source: TRAI Fair Usage Policy framework
required_correction: None — TRAI requires ISPs/TSPs to clearly disclose FUP thresholds and the post-FUP throttled speed (e.g., some plans drop to as low as 64kbps or similar reduced tiers after the data cap), confirming this is standard, regulator-acknowledged practice in India.

article_title: How to Tell If Your Internet Plan Is Actually Giving You the Speed You Pay For
claim: A phone connected to 2.4GHz instead of 5GHz will cap out well below what a fast plan can deliver.
source: IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi standard throughput characteristics (widely documented across networking vendor and standards literature)
required_correction: None — this is standard, well-established Wi-Fi networking behavior: 2.4GHz channels are narrower and more congestion-prone with lower maximum theoretical throughput than 5GHz under the same Wi-Fi generation, so a device pinned to 2.4GHz will bottleneck below what a fast fiber/broadband plan can deliver even with a wired connection performing at full speed.

article_title: How to Tell If Your Internet Plan Is Actually Giving You the Speed You Pay For
claim: Many providers' own status-check apps show everything as fine even during a genuine outage affecting a specific area, since that status often reflects general network health rather than an individual connection.
required_correction: Plausible and consistent with general complaints about ISP status pages, but no specific Indian ISP's app/status-page behavior was documented as a source — this reads as a generalized claim rather than a demonstrated pattern for any named provider. Should be attributed as anecdotal or softened.

article_title: How to Tell If Your Internet Plan Is Actually Giving You the Speed You Pay For
claim: Porting a broadband connection to a different ISP has become considerably less painful than it used to be in most Indian cities.
required_correction: No specific regulatory change, process, or data point was found to substantiate a general improvement in broadband ISP-switching ease across Indian cities (unlike mobile number portability, which is a defined TRAI-regulated process, wired broadband switching is simply a new-connection signup with no formal 'porting' mechanism). Should be softened or removed unless a specific supporting change can be cited.

article_title: How to Set Up a Smart Plug and What It Is Actually Useful For
claim: Your home Wi-Fi network selected during setup must be 2.4GHz — most smart plugs don't support 5GHz.
source: General IoT/smart-home device hardware limitation, consistently documented across manufacturer support content and troubleshooting guides
required_correction: None — this is accurate and a well-documented, near-universal limitation of budget/mid-range Wi-Fi smart plugs, which typically include only a 2.4GHz radio for cost, range, and wall-penetration reasons; 5GHz-capable smart plugs exist but remain a minority, dual-band premium option.

article_title: How to Set Up a Smart Plug and What It Is Actually Useful For
claim: Some routers merge 2.4GHz and 5GHz under a single network name, automatically switching devices between the two, which interferes with smart plug pairing since the plug needs a stable 2.4GHz connection during setup.
source: Widely documented router band-steering behavior (consistent across smart-home device troubleshooting guides)
required_correction: None — 'band steering' (merging 2.4GHz/5GHz under one SSID) is a real, common router feature, and it is a well-documented, frequent cause of IoT pairing failures industry-wide, since setup mode on most smart plugs specifically needs the phone to briefly join the plug's own 2.4GHz-only temporary hotspot and then hand off 2.4GHz credentials.

article_title: How to Set Up a Smart Plug and What It Is Actually Useful For
claim: Using an underrated smart plug for a heavy appliance is a genuine fire risk, not just a device failure risk.
source: General electrical safety consensus (NFPA/CPSC-style guidance cited across consumer electrical-safety reporting) — no single Indian regulator (BIS) statement located specifically on smart plugs
required_correction: The underlying physics (sustained near-max-rated current load generates heat, and undersized switching contacts/wiring can overheat and ignite) is an established electrical safety principle backed by fire-safety agencies internationally. However, no specific Indian BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards) advisory on smart plugs specifically was found — cite it as a general electrical safety principle rather than implying a specific Indian regulatory warning exists.

article_title: How to Set Up a Smart Plug and What It Is Actually Useful For
claim: A smart plug, being a small always-on internet-connected device, draws a small amount of standby power itself to stay connected and responsive to commands.
source: Independent measurements/reporting on smart plug idle power draw (e.g. SlashGear, Robots.net summarizing manufacturer/teardown data)
required_correction: None on the core claim — independent measurements consistently show smart plugs draw roughly 1-5 watts idle to stay connected to Wi-Fi and respond to commands, supporting the article's point that the plug's own standby draw should be weighed against the standby savings it provides.

article_title: How to Set Up a Smart Plug and What It Is Actually Useful For
claim: A smart plug can't read an appliance's own internal state — a fan set to a speed before being switched off will resume at that same speed when power returns, and a water heater's thermostat still governs temperature regardless of the plug's schedule.
source: Basic electrical/appliance engineering principle — a smart plug only switches mains power, it has no data connection to the appliance's internal controls
required_correction: None — this is a straightforward, accurate description of how a simple on/off relay smart plug interacts (or doesn't) with an appliance's own internal electronics; it has no way to communicate with or alter the appliance's internal settings.

article_title: How to Set Up a Smart Plug and What It Is Actually Useful For
claim: Some budget smart plugs forget their configured schedule after a full power outage and revert to a default state once power returns.
required_correction: Plausible for some budget models (schedule storage implementation varies by chipset/firmware) but no specific model or manufacturer source was found confirming this as a documented, common behavior versus an occasional/anecdotal one. Present as 'check the specific model's behavior' rather than a general rule, which the article already partly does — but the underlying premise itself remains unsourced.

article_title: How to Set Up a Smart Plug and What It Is Actually Useful For
claim: Power monitoring lets you see that an old fridge or a poorly maintained AC can draw far more than people assume.
required_correction: Reasonable, generally true observation about appliance efficiency degradation, but stated as a general assumption without specific wattage data or a cited study, so treat as editorial framing rather than a checkable statistic.

article_title: How to Set Up a Home Wi-Fi Guest Network, and Why You Should
claim: A guest network is a second Wi-Fi name broadcast from the same router, isolated from the main network at the traffic level, so guest devices generally can't see or access devices on the main network.
source: TP-Link official support/blog documentation on guest networks and AP isolation
required_correction: None — this matches how mainstream router vendors (TP-Link, and similarly Netgear, Asus, etc.) implement and document guest networks: traffic isolation from the main LAN is the defining feature, when the isolation setting is properly enabled (see next claim).

article_title: How to Set Up a Home Wi-Fi Guest Network, and Why You Should
claim: Simply creating a second network name without turning off local network access defeats most of the purpose — the separate name alone doesn't create isolation, a specific setting does.
source: TP-Link official support documentation on guest network / 'Allow guest to access local network' setting
required_correction: None — TP-Link's own documentation confirms a distinct toggle (e.g., 'Allow guest network access to local network', or 'Allow Local Access' in AP/mesh modes) separate from simply enabling the guest network SSID, and this setting must be explicitly disabled for isolation to actually take effect. This pattern is consistent across other major router brands as well.

article_title: How to Set Up a Home Wi-Fi Guest Network, and Why You Should
claim: Router admin panels are commonly accessed by typing the router's IP address, commonly 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1, into a browser.
source: Netgear and TP-Link official router login documentation
required_correction: None — 192.168.1.1 and 192.168.0.1 are the most common default gateway/admin addresses across major consumer router brands (TP-Link, Netgear, D-Link, and others), consistent with official vendor login documentation. Some brands and ISP-supplied routers use other defaults (e.g., 192.168.8.1, 10.0.0.1, or a vendor-specific address), which the article could briefly note.

article_title: How to Set Up a Home Wi-Fi Guest Network, and Why You Should
claim: Smart plugs, bulbs, cheap security cameras, and similar IoT devices are frequently less secure than a phone or laptop, since many run outdated software and their manufacturers don't push updates reliably.
source: FTC 2022 report on router/IoT security; industry research on unpatched IoT firmware
required_correction: None on the core claim — this is well documented: the FTC's 2022 router security report found many devices ship with automatic updates disabled by default and most residential users never manually update them, and independent industry research estimates roughly 60% of IoT devices lack proper update mechanisms or timely patching, supporting the claim that IoT devices are a relatively weaker security link than general-purpose computers/phones.

article_title: How to Set Up a Home Wi-Fi Guest Network, and Why You Should
claim: Very old or budget routers sometimes implement guest networks poorly, either not fully isolating traffic despite the setting being enabled, or requiring a firmware update to fix known bugs.
required_correction: Plausible given general consumer router quality variance and scattered community-forum reports of guest-network isolation bugs on specific models, but no authoritative source quantifying this as a widespread or common failure mode was found. Present as a reason to test isolation manually (which the article correctly recommends) rather than as an established, sourced fact.

article_title: How to Set Up a Home Wi-Fi Guest Network, and Why You Should
claim: Some newer routers support a time-limited guest credential that expires automatically after a set number of hours.
source: General router feature availability (e.g., mesh systems such as Google Nest Wifi / eero offering scheduled or temporary guest access) — no single comprehensive vendor index found
required_correction: The feature exists on some modern mesh/consumer router platforms (temporary or scheduled guest network access), so the claim is directionally accurate, but it isn't universal across 'newer routers' generally — many current mid-range routers still lack auto-expiring guest credentials. Recommend checking the specific model's feature list rather than assuming it broadly on newer hardware.
